shots.narration: You're born in Rome, in the year 31, and you already have an owner.
shots.notes: Crane down onto mother cradling a swaddled baby (baby implied in her arms). Joy flips to dread on 'owner'.

shots.narration: It isn't your mother. It isn't your father. It's the emperor.
shots.notes: Whip from the quarters to an EMPTY imperial couch guarded by a praetorian. Emperor in AD 31 is not Claudius, so no emperor is shown.

shots.narration: Your mother is a slave in the imperial household, which makes you one too.
shots.notes: Slow push on mother holding the baby; other enslaved staff in background, heads down.

shots.narration: The Romans have a word for a baby like you: verna. A slave born in the house.

infographic.title: VERNA
infographic.sub: born a slave, in the house

shots.notes: Script cue: INFOGRAPHIC CARD 'VERNA = born a slave, in the house'.

shots.narration: In the eyes of the law, you're property, the same as the furniture.
shots.notes: Emotional turn. Accountant lists the baby in the same ledger as a stool and a lamp.

shots.narration: Nobody asks what you think. You're three days old.
shots.notes: Deadpan beat. Orbit around mother and the tiny bundle.

shots.narration: The palace is enormous. Cooks, doorkeepers, accountants, and people whose only job is the emperor's clothes.
shots.notes: FLOATING TAGS over workers. Scribe already tagged ACCOUNTANT; maid carries a folded toga.

shots.narration: Everyone has a role. Everyone is replaceable.
shots.notes: Slow-mo: one servant is waved out of line, an identical one steps into the same slot.

shots.narration: You grow up in the corridors, learning the rules before you learn to read.
shots.notes: Child version of YOU (scale 0.7) trotting down a corridor past adults.

shots.narration: Walk fast. Look down. Never touch the food.
shots.notes: Mother counts the rules on her fingers; child shrinks with each one.

shots.narration: That last rule matters. Because in this house, food is not just food.
shots.notes: MACRO INSERT: plate of mushrooms on a polished table, warm light.

shots.narration: The thing is, powerful Romans have a habit of dying at dinner.
shots.notes: Goblet tips over on an empty dining couch; staff in background freeze. No victim shown.

shots.narration: A cup of wine, a plate of mushrooms, and the empire changes hands before dessert.
shots.notes: Whip across staff staring at the empty couch, then at each other.

shots.narration: So the palace has a solution: someone who eats first.
shots.notes: A taster takes a bite while a guard watches him like a hawk.

shots.narration: Years pass, and you turn nineteen. One morning, a tired freedman studies you for a long time, then asks one question.
shots.notes: Adult YOU now. Scribe rig plays the tired freedman (role change tag). Long, awkward stare.

shots.narration: "Do you have a strong stomach?" You nod.
shots.notes: Emotional turn: YOU nod eagerly. Bad idea.

shots.narration: Wrong answer.
shots.notes: Script AKIRA cutaway (deadpan). Only 2 words: hold ~1.6 s.

shots.narration: Congratulations. You're now a praegustator. And your job is to take the risk, so the emperor doesn't have to.
shots.notes: Role change tag PRAEGUSTATOR. AD 50: emperor is Claudius, relaxed because someone else drinks first.

shots.narration: Of course, that's the short version. The long version starts with a jug of water.
shots.notes: MACRO on the plain clay cold-water jug (motif 1).

shots.narration: And for one person, at one dinner, it ends with a jug of water too.
shots.notes: Torchlit flash-forward. Ominous tilt; nobody else shown. Do not reveal who.

shots.narration: But let's back up. Before you ever eat for the emperor, you carry his water.
shots.notes: Rewind whip back to childhood. Child YOU struggles beside a huge jug.

shots.narration: Here's something about Roman dinners. Nobody serious drinks wine straight. It gets mixed with water.
shots.notes: Servant mixes wine and water; second servant raises an eyebrow at anyone drinking it neat.

shots.narration: Hot drinks get cooled down with water too.
shots.notes: Cook blows on a steaming bowl, unimpressed.

shots.narration: So at every meal, somewhere in the palace, somebody has to carry the cold water. That somebody is you.
shots.notes: Emotional turn on 'you': background staff all point at the child.

shots.narration: It's a clay jug almost half your size.
shots.notes: MACRO INSERT: cold-water jug, beaded with water; child beside it for scale.

shots.narration: You carry it from the kitchen, down the corridor, past the guards, and you set it down exactly where you're told.
shots.notes: Dolly alongside the child hugging the jug past two guards.

shots.narration: Not near the food. Never near the food. In winter it numbs your fingers.
shots.notes: Child sets the jug far from the platters; guard watches. Breath fog / shiver on winter line.

shots.narration: In summer it sweats more than you do. Remember this jug.
shots.notes: Both the jug and the child drip. Push in on the jug on 'Remember this jug'.

shots.narration: It's coming back, years from now, on the worst night of your life.
shots.notes: Torchlit flash-forward, adult YOU in shadow. Same framing as B01_S20.

shots.narration: Your mother works in the wardrobe. She folds, mends and carries the emperor's clothes.
shots.notes: Close on mother's hands mending a purple-trimmed toga.

shots.narration: And she teaches you the three lessons that keep a palace slave out of trouble.
shots.notes: Mother kneels to child's level.

shots.narration: Be useful. Be quiet. Be somewhere else when things go wrong.
shots.notes: Three fingers, one per lesson.

shots.narration: She also teaches you to read a room before you walk into it.
shots.notes: Both peek around a doorway before entering.

shots.narration: Who's angry. Who's tired. Who's about to need something you'd better already be holding.
shots.notes: Whip across three faces (angry guard, tired accountant, needy maid) back to child holding a jug.

shots.narration: The palace is a small city, and everyone in it has a slot.
shots.notes: Fly through a busy corridor; each worker in their own slot.

shots.narration: Cooks feed it. Doorkeepers guard it. Accountants count it. Your mother dresses it.
shots.notes: Script cue: INFOGRAPHIC CARD 'WHO RUNS THE PALACE'. Reveal items one per sentence.

shots.narration: And you carry its water, which puts you at the bottom of a very tall ladder.
shots.notes: Low angle from child's height; adults loom behind like rungs of a ladder.

shots.narration: So where does that leave you? Right where the law put you on day three.
shots.notes: Callback to the furniture ledger.

shots.narration: Property. Property gets fed, housed and moved around.
shots.notes: Accountant ticks the child off a list and points him elsewhere.

shots.narration: Property does not get asked whether it would like a different job. Hold that thought.
shots.notes: Deadpan 'Hold that thought': child looks at camera.

shots.narration: The kitchen is where you learn the big rule properly. Once, you reach for a crust of bread on a tray.
shots.notes: Cook's back is turned; child's hand drifts toward the bread.

shots.narration: Just a reach. The cook spots you from across the room.
shots.notes: Emotional turn: whip to the cook's glare.

shots.narration: You don't reach again. Because in this house, a hand near the food is a question.
shots.notes: Script cue BUBBLE, COOK. Child yanks hand back in slow motion.

shots.narration: Whose hand? Why? And what did it leave behind?
shots.notes: MACRO on the bread tray: suspicion, nothing visibly wrong.

shots.narration: By the time you're a teenager, the emperor is Claudius.
shots.notes: Teen YOU (scale 0.8). First proper look at Claudius.

shots.narration: He's older, and he's kind to you in a way nobody else up there is.
shots.notes: Claudius gives the teen a nod; guard in background does not.

shots.narration: He has one great weakness at the table. Mushrooms. You'll want to remember that too.
shots.notes: Punch in on 'Mushrooms'. Claudius delighted; teen uneasy.

shots.narration: And you notice one more thing. Before anything reaches the emperor's lips, someone else takes a bite first.
shots.notes: A taster bites first; Claudius waits. Plants the job.

shots.narration: Which brings us back to nineteen, and that question about your stomach.
shots.notes: Script cue STAMP. Back to the freedman's question.

shots.narration: The word is praegustator. It means "fore-taster": the person who tastes the food and drink before it reaches the master's table.
shots.notes: Script cue: INFOGRAPHIC CARD 'PRAEGUSTATOR = fore-taster'.

shots.narration: Prae, before. Gustare, to taste. The Romans named the job exactly what it is.
shots.notes: Latin split over YOU's head.

shots.narration: It might be the most honest thing in the building. So who does a job like this?
shots.notes: Deadpan.

shots.narration: Slaves, and freedmen. People with options do not apply.
shots.notes: Line-up of tasters. Nobody here volunteered.

shots.narration: And unlike the cooks or the accountants, you can't be quietly good at this job.
shots.notes: Cook and accountant quietly competent; YOU sweating.

shots.narration: Either nothing happens to you, or everybody finds out.
shots.notes: Everyone in the hall turns to stare at YOU at once. Implied only.

shots.narration: There are two rules, and they're simple. You taste everything. And you're not allowed to refuse.
shots.notes: Freedman lays down the two rules.

shots.narration: Remember when nobody asked whether you'd like a different job? This is the different job.
shots.notes: Callback to Beat 2.

shots.narration: Your training starts in the tasters' room. It's small and warm, and it smells like every meal of the day at once.
shots.notes: MACRO INSERT: steaming bowl in the tasters' room, then reveal YOU sniffing.

shots.narration: There's a bench, a shelf of cups, and a door that opens straight towards the dining room. Short commute. Very short.
shots.notes: Fly past bench and shelf, through the door: the dining room is right there.

shots.narration: On the shelf, every cup has been used by someone before you.
shots.notes: MACRO: worn cups on the shelf.

shots.narration: You try not to wonder where all those someones went. You fail.
shots.notes: Emotional turn on 'You fail'.

shots.narration: The man who tests you is Halotus, Claudius's taster. A eunuch.
shots.notes: Halotus intro, low angle.

shots.narration: Calm, quiet, impossible to read. He looks at a plate the way other people look at the weather.
shots.notes: Halotus studies a fruit plate.

shots.narration: He hands you a piece of bread. You chew. You swallow.
shots.notes: MACRO INSERT: Halotus' hand passes the bread; YOU's first test bite.

shots.narration: And then you do the actual job. You wait.
shots.notes: Hold on YOU, frozen.

shots.narration: Halotus watches you. You watch the wall. Somewhere, an oil lamp hisses.
shots.notes: Long silence from above.

shots.narration: A minute feels like an afternoon. Nothing happens.
shots.notes: Relief on 'Nothing happens'.

shots.narration: That's it. That's the test. In this profession, nothing happening is a perfect score.
shots.notes: Deadpan.

shots.narration: Wait. That was the entire training?

bubble.text: Wait. That was the entire training?

shots.notes: Script AKIRA cutaway (wide-eyed).

shots.narration: Halotus nods once, and moves on to the next plate. No speech. No welcome.
shots.notes: Halotus already busy.

shots.narration: Just more food, and more waiting.
shots.notes: MACRO on the next bowl.

shots.narration: You've just learned the most important skill of your career: standing perfectly still while you find out whether you're going to live.
shots.notes: Push in on a perfectly still, sweating YOU.

shots.narration: There's one more thing you learn that first week, and nobody has to tell you.
shots.notes: Walking alone.

shots.narration: People in this job don't get statues. They don't get speeches.
shots.notes: YOU look up at an empty plinth.

shots.narration: If they're lucky, they get a line carved on a stone. Almost nobody remembers them.
shots.notes: MACRO INSERT: chisel on a blank stone, pull back to YOU. Do NOT show the Zosimus stone yet (Beat 10 payoff).

shots.narration: Almost. We'll come back to that at the very end.
shots.notes: Turn on 'Almost'. Plant for the epilogue.

shots.narration: Then it's routine. Taste. Wait. Watch. Repeat.
shots.notes: MONTAGE cue (bowl, platter, goblet, bowl) starts here. One expression beat per word: taste, wait, watch, repeat.

shots.narration: Bread in the morning. Fish at midday. Sauces, fruit, wine.
shots.notes: MONTAGE continues (platter). Cook announces each course while YOU taste. Whip between courses.

shots.narration: You taste in small bites, you wait, you watch the faces at the table,
shots.notes: MONTAGE (goblet). Orbit the table. YOU study faces: Claudius content, guard suspicious.

shots.narration: and you try not to look like you're watching your own stomach.
shots.notes: Continues the sentence from S03. YOU glance down at your stomach, then realise someone noticed.

shots.narration: Some days you taste for the emperor. Some days for his guests.
shots.notes: MONTAGE ends on the second bowl. The guests are servant rigs with no tags, enjoying the food in the background.

shots.narration: Every plate gets the same treatment, because poison doesn't check the seating plan.
shots.notes: Top-down drift over the seating: the same small bite at every place, high or low status.

shots.narration: You learn the face Halotus makes when a dish is fine.
shots.notes: Halotus's one unreadable face. Keep his emotion identical in S08 for the joke.

shots.narration: It's the same face he makes when it isn't. That's not reassuring.
shots.notes: Same face as S07 on purpose. Emotional turn for YOU on 'not reassuring'.

shots.narration: The cold-water jug is always there, at the edge of every table you work.
shots.notes: MACRO INSERT cue: the cold-water jug at the edge of the table (motif 2). YOU are soft in the background.

shots.narration: Same clay. Same shape. You carried it for years. Now you barely see it.
shots.notes: Dolly with YOU as you walk past the jug without a glance.

shots.narration: That's going to turn out to be a mistake.
shots.notes: Torch-lit flash-forward with the same framing as B01_S20 and B02_S09. Warm torchlight, never dark blue. Do not reveal who or what.

shots.narration: Here's the uncomfortable part. The ancient sources barely say how tasters were supposed to detect poison.
shots.notes: The accountant searches a scroll for instructions and shrugs. Show no detection method on screen (F14).

shots.narration: There's no reliable test. No trick. No gadget. There's just you.
shots.notes: Emotional turn on 'just you'.

shots.narration: If you're fine, the food is fine. If you're not fine, well, the food has been reviewed.
shots.notes: Dark joke, implied only. Slow motion as another taster hesitates mid-bite. Nobody falls on screen.

shots.narration: So the safety system is... YOU?

bubble.text: So the safety system is... YOU?

shots.notes: Script AKIRA cutaway (shout).

shots.narration: So you invent your own little systems, like everyone does. You chew slowly.
shots.notes: MACRO on one slow, careful bite.

shots.narration: You count your breaths. You watch the cook's face when a plate goes out.
shots.notes: YOU study the cook. The cook stares back, unimpressed.

shots.narration: None of it works. All of it helps you feel like you're doing something.
shots.notes: Deadpan.

shots.narration: The old tasters pass the time with stories. Their favourite is one Pliny tells.
shots.notes: Storytime on the bench. Felix (already tagged in S14) tells it. Hilarus grins because it is his favourite.

shots.narration: Mark Antony wouldn't touch food that hadn't been tasted. Cleopatra tricked him with poisoned flowers anyway.
shots.notes: [UNCERTAIN] Pliny's story (F12-F13). Antony and Cleopatra have no rig ids, so this is a card only.

shots.narration: The old tasters laugh. You laugh too, a little late.
shots.notes: Whip to YOU joining the laugh a beat late.

shots.narration: Because the moral isn't funny. Being careful isn't the same as being safe.
shots.notes: Emotional turn. The laughter dies and the room goes quiet.

shots.narration: Most days, there's nothing to report. Nobody slumps. Nobody shouts.
shots.notes: Peaceful dinner seen from above.

shots.narration: The plates go out, the plates come back, and you eat your own dinner standing up, cold, last.
shots.notes: Fly through the busy kitchen to YOU eating alone from a cold bowl.

shots.narration: Months become years. You get very good at boring. In this job, boring is the goal.
shots.notes: Time-lapse feel: light sweeps across the room. No stamp, because the script gives no year.

shots.narration: You put the old story out of your mind. The year 54 is coming, and so are the mushrooms.
shots.notes: Cliffhanger into Beat 5: macro push onto the mushroom platter. Relief turns to dread on 'The year 54'.

shots.narration: In the year 54, according to Roman writers, Claudius sits down to a dish of mushrooms. His favourite.
shots.notes: Claudius delighted, Halotus unreadable (same face as B04).

shots.narration: His taster is Halotus. What happens next depends on who you ask, and the Romans themselves couldn't agree.
Version one comes from Tacitus. A woman named Locusta, a specialist in exactly this kind of problem,
shots.notes: Script cue infographic.

shots.narration: allegedly prepares poison for the empress Agrippina. And Halotus serves it.
shots.notes: Implied only, no vial or method shown.

shots.narration: Version two comes from Suetonius. It's Halotus again, at a banquet with the priests.
Version three also comes from Suetonius, who apparently couldn't pick. There's no banquet.
It's a family dinner, and Agrippina serves Claudius the mushrooms herself.
And one more account puts the blame on the emperor's doctor.
One emperor, one plate of mushrooms, and at least three versions of the evening.
Every one of them is an allegation. None of them is a verdict.
For someone in your line of work, though, the versions share one uncomfortable detail.
In two of the three, the poison allegedly goes through the emperor's own taster.
The man who tested you. The job that is supposed to stop this exact thing
is standing right in the middle of it.
Three versions. Zero confessions.
shots.notes: Script AKIRA cutaway.

shots.narration: Where are you that night? Close enough to see. Not close enough to know.
You see Claudius eat. You see him go quiet. You see him helped away from the table.
And you see Halotus, standing exactly where a taster stands, with exactly the face he always has.
According to the Roman writers, Claudius never recovers. Whether it was poison, and whose, is something nobody will ever settle.
Remember that joke about the empire changing hands before dessert? It turns out it wasn't much of a joke.
The new emperor is young Nero, Agrippina's son. He's relaxed. He smiles a lot.
And later, he makes a little joke about the whole affair. Mushrooms, he says, are "the food of the gods."
Let that sit for a second. Then stop thinking about it, because you work here,
and thinking is how people stop working here.
As for Halotus, according to ancient sources, he isn't punished. He keeps his post.
He just goes on tasting, for the new emperor now, with the same calm face.
You get a new post too. It's the best thing that ever happens to you. Give it a few months.
You're assigned to the children's table.
In the palace, the imperial children eat at their own table, a plainer one, set where the family can see them.
Simpler dishes, smaller cups. And every bite, every drink, is tested by a taster
chosen from the prince's own attendants. That's you now.
Your table is plainer, but it isn't private. The children eat in full view of the family,
which means every bite you take is watched by the most powerful people in Rome.
You learn to taste with your whole face perfectly still. A frown could start a panic. A smile could start a rumour.
The prince is Britannicus. He's thirteen, he's the late emperor's son,
and he is the first person you've ever tasted for who actually says thank you.
He's polite. He asks your name. He remembers it the next day, which in this building is practically a scandal.
He likes his drinks hot. So you test them hot. You burn your tongue about once a week.
It's the only workplace injury of your career you're happy to have.
Sometimes he sings. Not for an audience. Not for anyone important. Just a boy singing at a table,
while the adults around him go suspiciously quiet.
You never learn the words. You don't need to. You just know it's the best sound in the building.
For a while, life at the plainer table is good. The food is simple. The danger feels far away.
You start to think the children's table might be the safest posting in the palace. Who would bother with a kid?
You do notice how the grown-up table watches the little one.
Nero laughs easily. His smile reaches everyone in the room. It's just hard to tell what's behind it.
Your mother says you look happier. She's right. These are your best months.
And then it's the year 55. An ordinary dinner. Ordinary hot drinks. And an ordinary jug of cold water.
This is the evening as Tacitus tells it.
The family is at the main table. The children are at theirs.
You're standing where you always stand, beside Britannicus, close enough to reach his cup.
He's in a good mood. He's been talking all evening, about nothing much, the way thirteen-year-olds do.
You've heard every story twice. You don't mind.
A drink arrives for him. It's very hot. Steam rises off the top.
You taste it first, the way you always do. It burns, the way it always does. Then you wait.
Nothing happens. It's harmless. You know it is, because you're still standing. You hand it to him.
Around you, the dinner carries on. Cups clink at the main table. Somebody laughs at something.
A servant crosses behind you with a tray.
It's the kind of evening you've stood through a hundred times, the kind you'd forget by morning.
Britannicus lifts the cup, and puts it straight back down. Too hot, he says.
That's normal. Hot drinks get cooled down. That's what the water is for.
The jug. The cup. The wait.
shots.notes: MACRO: jug, cup, a hand at the edge of frame. No pouring detail.

shots.narration: It's the same kind of jug you carried as a child. The jug you stopped seeing years ago.
Britannicus drinks. He goes quiet. He slumps at the table. He doesn't get up.
shots.notes: By implication only.

shots.narration: At the main table, Nero stays where he is. He tells the guests it's nothing to worry about.
Just one of Britannicus's epileptic fits.
You're still standing beside the empty space where the cup was. Your mouth still tastes of the hot drink. You're fine.
shots.notes: Slow push on the empty cup, characters out of focus.

shots.narration: That's when you understand. And it's worse than you think.
Tacitus gives a reason for the way it was done. It was arranged, in his words,
so that "the usage might not be dropped or the crime betrayed by the death of both prince and attendant."

infographic.title: TACITUS ON THE PLAN
infographic.sub: why the taster had to live

shots.notes: Quote from the research doc.

shots.narration: The attendant is you. Not you by name. Nobody needed your name.
Just the role. The taster. The one who has to be standing at the end.
The plan didn't go around you. It was built around you.
If you had fallen too, everyone would have known. So you had to live. Your survival was the cover story.
You think of the old tasters and their story about the poisoned flowers.
shots.notes: Memory: they laugh, YOU do not.

shots.narration: Being careful was never the same as being safe. Now you know exactly how far apart those two things are.
That same night, Britannicus is cremated. Fast. Quiet. Done before morning.
You go back to your quarters. Your mother is waiting. She doesn't ask what happened. She already knows.
She taught you the rule herself: be somewhere else when things go wrong. Tonight, you weren't somewhere else.
The next morning, the palace is quiet. Not grieving quiet. Careful quiet.
shots.notes: Quiet, watchful morning in the sunlit palace corridor.

shots.narration: People speak softly. Nobody says his name.
shots.notes: Staff whisper in hushed tones while avoiding eye contact.

shots.narration: The servants move a little faster, and nobody looks at the children's table, which is suddenly one chair emptier.
shots.notes: The remaining children sit quietly beside the noticeably empty spot while servants hurry past.

shots.narration: Nobody blames you. That's the point. You did your job perfectly.
shots.notes: Punch-in on the protagonist realizing there is no blame because the job was done exactly by the rules.

shots.narration: You tasted the drink, and the drink was fine. You keep your post.
shots.notes: Low angle emphasizing the heavy reality of keeping the post.

shots.narration: Good news: you're not fired. That's the bad news.

bubble.text: Good news: you're not fired. That's the bad news.

shots.notes: Akira cutaway delivering the dry punchline deadpan.

shots.narration: And you're not the only one. Here's who else gets to keep their job.

infographic.title: STILL EMPLOYED
infographic.sub: Who else gets to keep their job

shots.notes: Infographic card listing the four who stay employed.

shots.narration: Locusta, the woman named in the Claudius story.
shots.notes: Torch-lit night cutaway introducing Locusta in the shadowed palace kitchen.

shots.narration: According to ancient writers, she goes on working during Nero's reign. Nobody seems in any hurry to stop her.
shots.notes: Locusta remains calmly at work under Nero while guards and scribes look away.

shots.narration: Halotus. Still calm. Still unreadable. Still tasting for the emperor, as if the year 54 was just another dinner.
shots.notes: Halotus stands composed beside Nero and a mushroom platter.

shots.narration: And the cold-water jugs. They're still on every table.
shots.notes: Macro close-up pushing directly onto a cold-water jug sitting on the banquet table.

shots.narration: Somebody still carries them. Somebody still sets them down exactly where they're told.
shots.notes: Top-down drift watching servants quietly place jugs along the tables.

shots.narration: You go back to work, because there is nothing else to go back to. Taste, wait, watch.
shots.notes: Returning to the daily kitchen routine of tasting and waiting.

shots.narration: Except now you watch differently. You watch hands. You watch jugs.
shots.notes: Emotional turn: punch-in as the taster's eyes dart suspiciously across servants and jugs.

shots.narration: You watch what happens after you've handed the cup over,
shots.notes: Camera tracks past the handed-off goblet toward the table.

shots.narration: the one part of the meal that was never your job.
shots.notes: Uneasy dutch tilt highlighting the blind spot outside the taster's authority.

shots.narration: The rules haven't changed. You taste everything. You're not allowed to refuse.
shots.notes: Orbit around the taster trapped by the rigid rules of the household.

shots.narration: And now you know what tasting everything really proves. Not that the food is safe.
shots.notes: Macro push into the rim of the tasting goblet.

shots.narration: Only that it was safe at the moment you swallowed.
shots.notes: Slow-motion impact emphasizing the chilling limit of the taster's test.

shots.narration: Some nights you replay the moment you handed him the cup. The heat. The wait.
shots.notes: Torch-lit memory replay of handing the steaming cup to Britannicus.

shots.narration: His voice saying it was too hot. You never find the mistake, because there wasn't one.
shots.notes: Emotional turn in memory: cold water tips in as the taster realizes there was never a mistake to fix.

shots.narration: You did everything right. That's what keeps you awake.
shots.notes: Sleepless torch-lit night in the tasters' room.

shots.narration: Years go by like this. Quietly. Carefully. You get older.
shots.notes: Steady corridor dolly conveying the careful passage of years.

shots.narration: Nobody poisons you. In this job, that counts as a career highlight.
shots.notes: Whip-right dry humor beat celebrating simply staying unpoisoned.

shots.narration: And somewhere in the back of your mind, a number keeps getting closer. Thirty.
shots.notes: Tight macro push building quiet hope toward the age of thirty.

shots.narration: In the emperor's household, slaves are routinely freed somewhere between the ages of thirty and thirty-five.
shots.notes: Establishing the administrative room where imperial household manumissions are recorded.

shots.narration: You make it to about thirty-three. One day, it's official. You're free.
shots.notes: Emotional turn: punch-in with age stamp as official freedom arrives.

shots.narration: You get a new name, too. You take the family name of the house that owned you.
shots.notes: Walking the sunlit corridor as the scribe explains the new freedman name.

shots.narration: So now you're Tiberius Claudius, with your old slave name tacked on the end, like a receipt.
shots.notes: Role-change tag reveals the new Roman freedman identity with dry amusement.

shots.narration: Freedom in the palace is a strange thing.
shots.notes: Top-down drift showing the protagonist still inside the same palace walls.

shots.narration: Some imperial freedmen go on to become powerful officials, men with offices, staff and real influence.
shots.notes: Confident imperial freedmen directing staff inside busy palace offices.

shots.narration: Others just keep doing the same work under a better name.
shots.notes: Whip-right contrast back to ordinary palace workers doing the exact same chores.

shots.narration: You're somewhere in the middle. You still know the taste of every sauce in the building.
shots.notes: Experienced freedman calmly inspecting kitchen sauces.

shots.narration: But for the first time in your life, your stomach legally belongs to you.
shots.notes: Warm punch-in on genuine personal relief.

shots.narration: The first thing you do as a free person is eat a meal that nobody else has tasted,
shots.notes: Quiet, unhurried orbit around the protagonist sitting alone with a simple plate.

shots.narration: and nobody else is waiting on. It's bread. It's ordinary.
shots.notes: Macro close-up on the plain, ordinary loaf of bread.

shots.narration: You still stop before the first bite. You still wait.
shots.notes: Instinctive slow-motion pause before taking a bite of his own bread.

shots.narration: Old habits are hard to break when they're the reason you're alive.
shots.notes: Soft, bittersweet acceptance before finally eating.

shots.narration: You visit your mother. She's older now, slower, still folding the emperor's clothes.
shots.notes: Gentle reunion in the laundry quarters where mother still works.

shots.narration: She looks at your new name for a long time, as if it might be a trick.
shots.notes: Mother inspects the manumission name with wary palace instincts.

shots.narration: Then she tells you she always knew you'd be useful. From her, that's practically a poem.
shots.notes: Heartwarming punch-in as mother offers her highest form of praise.

shots.narration: And Halotus? According to ancient sources, his career outlasts Nero himself.
shots.notes: Whip-right tonal shift back to Halotus standing poised as Nero fades.

shots.narration: Emperors come and go. The man at the centre of the mushroom story just keeps landing on his feet.
shots.notes: Dutch punch spotlighting Halotus's uncanny political survival.

shots.narration: That's the real skill in this house. Not a strong stomach. Being useful to whoever comes next.
shots.notes: Macro push on the imperial goblet framing Halotus and the protagonist behind it.

shots.narration: Which leaves one question. What happens to people like you, in the end? Who remembers a taster?
shots.notes: Reflective top-down drift posing the closing question.

shots.narration: As it turns out, one of them made sure he'd be remembered. In stone.
shots.notes: Fly-through transition into the sunlit stone-carver's yard.

shots.narration: You were never a real person. But the job was real. And so was he.
shots.notes: Soft daylight crane-down in the stone-carver's yard separating fiction from history.

shots.narration: His name was Tiberius Claudius Zosimus. An imperial freedman, with the same family name you were given.
shots.notes: Punch-in introducing the real historical freedman Tiberius Claudius Zosimus.

shots.narration: He served the emperor Domitian, as one of the men who ate first.
shots.notes: Orbit around Zosimus performing the ancient duty of eating first.

shots.narration: His tombstone was found at Mainz, the Roman town of Mogontiacum.
shots.notes: Slow push in the stone-carver's yard locating the Mainz tombstone.

shots.narration: It dates to around the year 83, when Domitian was campaigning against the Chatti.
shots.notes: Frontier campaign framing with date and place stamp.

shots.narration: Even at the edge of the empire, someone still had to eat first.
shots.notes: Lateral dolly underscoring that imperial food tasting followed the emperor even to the frontier.

shots.narration: You can see it today, in the Landesmuseum Mainz. And carved into it is the word for his job.
shots.notes: Top-down drift admiring the carved Latin inscription.

shots.narration: The word that once meant "take the risk, so the emperor doesn't have to."
shots.notes: Whip-right linking the fictional taster and real Zosimus across the meaning of the title.

shots.narration: Praegustator. Cut in stone, like something to be proud of.
shots.notes: Macro close-up celebrating the title cut permanently in stone.

shots.narration: Nobody wrote a history about him. Nobody wrote one about you, either.
shots.notes: Quiet, respectful slow push as both tasters stand side by side.

shots.narration: But somebody decided that word belonged on his grave,
shots.notes: Warm daylight orbit honoring the decision to preserve his title.

shots.narration: and it's still there, almost two thousand years later. Not bad, for a praegustator.
shots.notes: Final warm daylight closing shot honoring Zosimus and every forgotten praegustator.
